parrafos: Fast fashion is a business model in textile manufacturing where companies quickly create and sell clothing and footwear at affordable prices by replicating the latest fashion trends and designs using cheap and fast mass production techniques. Fast fashion is defined by Merriam-Webster as "an approach to the design, creation, and marketing of clothing fashions that emphasizes making fashion trends quickly and cheaply available to consumers."
Multinational retailers that employ the fast fashion strategy include Shein, Temu, Halara, Semir H&M, Primark, ASOS, Peacocks, Fashion Nova, Forever 21, Uniqlo, Edikted, Zaraand C&A.
As of 2026, 36% of clothing purchases worldwide are of the fast fashion category. The total market size of fast fashion clothing sales is estimated at $178 billion in sales per year.

Fast fashion brands have faced legal and regulatory issues due to alleged exploitation of labour, use of dangerous goods in their products, greenwashing their environmental impacts, and violations of intellectual property laws.

Fast fashion brands aim to put popular styles on the market as quickly as possible at a lower price than their competitors via optimized supply chains and quick response manufacturing methods. These retailers produce and sell products in small batches, maintain surplus manufacturing capacity to adjust production levels, use category management organization, and are able to make substantial and immediate adjustments to manufacturing based on sales. Fast fashion companies generally invest heavily in marketing, particularly via social media, using influencers and internet celebrities to promote their brand.

Before the 19th century, fashion was a laborious, time-consuming process that required sourcing raw materials like wool, cotton, or leather, weaving the natural fibers into fabric, and then fashioning the fabric into functional garments. However, the Industrial Revolution changed the world of fashion by introducing new technology like the sewing machine and textile machines.

As a result, clothes became cheaper and easier to make and buy. Localized dressmaking businesses emerged, catering to members of the middle class, and employing workroom employees along with garment workers, who worked from home for meager wages. These dress shops were early prototypes of the so-called 'sweatshops' that would become the foundation for twenty-first-century clothing production.

Fast fashion originated with utility clothing and tailors who sold mass-produced affordable suits for men. In the 1960s, companies including Inditex and Chelsea Girl attained commercial acumen, but the brand Biba endured as a fast fashion icon.

Before the popularization of the fast fashion model, the fashion industry traditionally operated on a four-season cycle, with designers working months in advance to anticipate customer preferences. However, this approach underwent a significant transformation in the 1960s and 1970s, as the younger generations began to create new trends. During this period there was still a clear distinction between luxury goods and High Street fashion.

Fast fashion grew during the late 20th century as the clothing industry adopted cheaper manufacturing techniques including more efficient supply chains, new quick response manufacturing methods, increased usage of low-cost labor from Asia, and cheaper petroleum-based synthetic fibers.
In 2013, the Rana Plaza collapse in Bangladesh, the deadliest garment-related accident in world history, brought more attention to the safety impact of the fast fashion industry.

In the 2010s and 2020s, fast fashion trends spread quicker via social media services such as Instagram and TikTok. This has led to an increase in the speed of production and trend cycles and a further decrease in quality of garments, some of which are encouraged to be worn only a few times before they are disposed of. This phenomenon has been dubbed ultra-fast fashion.. Many of the companies with a high social media presence, such as Shein, Fashion Nova, and PrettyLittleThing, promote ultra-fast fashion.

The high-volume and rapid-turnover model of fast fashion encourages consumers to purchase more clothes and replace them more frequently. According to the United Nations Environment Programme, consumers are buying approximately 60% more clothing than in the past while keeping garments for about half as long. The organization also reports that the equivalent of one truckload of discarded textiles is landfilled or incinerated every second.

Environmental pressures occur throughout the textile supply chain, from fibre production and dyeing to manufacturing, transportation, use and disposal. A scientific review published in 2020 estimated that the fashion industry produces more than 92 million tonnes of waste and consumes approximately 79 trillion litres of water annually. The review identified water consumption, chemical pollution, carbon emissions and textile waste as major environmental impacts associated with the industry.

The extensive use of synthetic fibres creates an additional source of pollution. Synthetic garments release microplastic fibres during their production, wearing, washing and disposal. The European Environment Agency estimates that between 200,000 and 500,000 tonnes of microplastics from textiles enter the global marine environment each year. Fast-fashion garments are associated with particularly high releases because synthetic fabrics tend to shed more fibres during their first washes, while these garments are generally used for shorter periods and often wear out quickly.

Researchers have argued that reducing these environmental impacts requires lower production volumes, more sustainable practices throughout the supply chain and longer garment lifespans. Reuse, improved textile collection and recycling can reduce waste, although these measures do not entirely prevent the release of microplastics from synthetic clothing.

Many fast fashion brands have faced legal and regulatory issues due to the exploitation of labour including poor pay and working conditions, including the use of sweatshops. In response, many brands audit supplier factories to ensure fair working conditions that are in compliance with local laws.

Many fast fashion brands have faced legal and regulatory issues since they produce clothing using non-biodegradable petroleum-based synthetic fibers and microplastics as well as dangerous goods including PFAS, endocrine disruptors, and carcinogens. They have been accused of greenwashing, hiding their true impact on carbon emissions and plastic pollution. Shein was fined €1m in Italy for misleading environmental claims about products. In response, some brands, such as H&M, have banned the use of PFAS and/or have purchased carbon offsets and credits and promoted textile recycling.

Fast fashion brands have been sued for copying designs that may violate intellectual property laws. In many lawsuits, fast fashion brands have been accused of copying designs, sometimes creating exact replicas, of major brands such as Ralph Lauren Corporation. Shein is considered to be the most frequent infringer; over 100 intellectual property-related lawsuits have been filed against Shein since 2017. Most such copyright lawsuits are settled confidentially. From 2019 to 2024, Shein paid $1.4 million to independent artists in settlements.

In June 2026, the French government enacted landmark legislation intended to regulate the fast fashion industry. The law–which took effect in September 2026–primarily targets "ultra-fast fashion" retailers that produce clothing at an "exceptionally" high volume with little incentive for repairability in comparison to a garment's cost. It places a levy on each article of clothing which must be paid to the producer responsibility organization Refashion (which will begin at €0.25–€12.00 per-article, and increase annually over the next four years to €2–€20 by 2030), and makes the products ineligible for tax credits on donating unsold goods. The law also requires that ultra-fast fashion retailers place public interest messages on all sale listings regarding the environmental and social impacts of fast fashion, including its production and shipment, and encouraging consumers to explore sustainable options. Beginning 1 January 2027, the law will also ban all advertising of ultra-fast fashion, including influencer marketing.

French trade minister Serge Papin stated that the law is intended primarily to target retailers such as AliExpress, Shein, and Temu. China's Ministry of Commerce demanded that the law be pulled, arguing that it was a discriminatory trade restriction, and warning that it will "take necessary measures to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises." French officials stated that they were willing to speak with China about the law and encouraged going through the World Trade Organisation, stating that "our Parliament is sovereign and has had its say. It has passed this law and we will fully respect its decision. This kind of threat, this challenge to a state's sovereign position, is coercion, economic retaliation. But for now, it remains a threat." The bill had also faced criticism from French lawmakers, including EELV MP Charles Fournier, for being "watered-down" through the legislative process to not target French and European companies such as H&M, Kiabi, and Zara.

In September 2026, the Green Party-led city council of Bristol, England passed a bylaw banning advertising for "high-carbon" products on city-controlled advertising spaces (such as billboards on bus stops), with the city notably classifying ultra-fast fashion as being covered by the law.
resumen_es: Explica el modelo de negocio de la moda rápida, su origen histórico, sus efectos sociales y ambientales y las respuestas legales recientes, como la ley francesa de 2026 contra la «moda ultrarrápida».

ideas_clave.idea: Fast fashion is a business model in which retailers such as Shein, H&M or Zara rapidly copy current trends and sell them cheaply thanks to quick mass production.
It accounts for over a third of clothing purchases worldwide, yet its brands face accusations over labour, hazardous substances, greenwashing and intellectual property.
Its competitive edge rests on flexible supply chains, small batches, spare capacity that reacts to sales and heavy promotion through social media influencers.
The Industrial Revolution made clothing cheaper to produce, and the low-paid workshops that emerged prefigured today's sweatshops.

Rooted in mass-produced utility clothing, the model replaced the traditional four-season calendar from the 1960s and expanded in the late twentieth century through cheap Asian labour and synthetic fibres.
The 2013 Rana Plaza disaster highlighted safety risks, while social networks have since accelerated trend cycles into lower-quality, disposable ultra-fast fashion.
The model fuels overconsumption, with people buying far more clothes and keeping them for less time, and the industry generates huge amounts of waste, water use and pollution.
Synthetic garments shed large quantities of microplastics, and experts call for lower volumes, longer-lasting clothes, reuse and recycling, although these do not fully solve the problem.
Brands have faced legal action for poor working conditions, harmful chemicals and misleading green claims, as well as for copying designs, Shein being the most frequent offender.
France passed a 2026 law imposing a rising levy, warning messages and an advertising ban on ultra-fast fashion, which China denounced as discriminatory while some French MPs found it too weak.
Bristol has also banned advertising of high-carbon products, including ultra-fast fashion, on city-controlled spaces.

resumen_modelo:
The text examines fast fashion, a business model whereby retailers such as Shein, H&M or Zara reproduce the latest trends at great speed and sell them at low prices thanks to cheap mass production. This segment now represents over a third of clothing purchases worldwide. Its success relies on highly responsive supply chains, small production runs adjusted to sales and intensive marketing on social media.

Historically, the Industrial Revolution made garments cheaper and gave rise to poorly paid workshops, the forerunners of modern sweatshops. From the 1960s onwards, the traditional four-season calendar gave way to faster cycles, and in the late twentieth century the sector expanded by relying on low-cost Asian labour and synthetic fibres. More recently, platforms such as Instagram and TikTok have accelerated trends further, giving rise to so-called ultra-fast fashion, with cheaper and more disposable clothes.

The consequences are considerable. Consumers buy around 60% more clothing than before but keep it for half as long, while the industry produces enormous quantities of waste, consumes vast amounts of water and releases microplastics, particularly from synthetic garments. Experts therefore advocate lower volumes and longer-lasting clothes. In addition, the sector faces lawsuits for labour exploitation, hazardous chemicals, greenwashing and design copying, following tragedies such as the Rana Plaza collapse in 2013.

Finally, public authorities have begun to react. In 2026 France adopted a law that imposes an increasing levy on each item, compulsory environmental warnings and, from 2027, an advertising ban on ultra-fast fashion. China condemned it as a discriminatory trade barrier, whereas some French lawmakers considered it watered down to spare European brands. Likewise, Bristol has banned advertisements for high-carbon products, including such clothing.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o no se dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Fast fashion represents more than a third of clothing purchases worldwide.
preguntas.cita: As of 2026, 36% of clothing purchases worldwide are of the fast fashion category.
preguntas.explicacion: Un 36 % es algo más de un tercio, así que la afirmación es verdadera.

preguntas.pregunta: How do fast fashion retailers organise their production?
opciones: They produce in small batches and keep spare capacity to adjust output
They produce in large batches planned a year in advance
They rely exclusively on local workshops
They avoid marketing on social media
respuestas: They produce in small batches and keep spare capacity to adjust output
preguntas.cita: These retailers produce and sell products in small batches, maintain surplus manufacturing capacity to adjust production levels
preguntas.explicacion: El texto habla de lotes pequeños y capacidad sobrante para ajustar la producción a las ventas. La planificación anual corresponde al modelo antiguo, y el texto dice que invierten mucho en redes sociales.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 6 una palabra que signifique «escaso, exiguo» (referido al salario).
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning “very small, inadequate” (about pay).
preguntas.cita: who worked from home for meager wages
preguntas.explicacion: «Meager» (en británico «meagre») significa escaso o miserable; se combina a menudo con «wages» o «income».

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o no se dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Before fast fashion became popular, the industry worked on a two-season cycle.
preguntas.cita: the fashion industry traditionally operated on a four-season cycle
preguntas.explicacion: El ciclo tradicional era de cuatro temporadas, no de dos. Se ha cambiado ese detalle.

preguntas.pregunta: Which of the following helped fast fashion grow in the late 20th century?
opciones: Greater use of low-cost labour from Asia
Higher tariffs on imported textiles
A return to natural fibres
Stricter safety regulations
respuestas: Greater use of low-cost labour from Asia
preguntas.cita: increased usage of low-cost labor from Asia, and cheaper petroleum-based synthetic fibers
preguntas.explicacion: El texto cita la mano de obra barata asiática y las fibras sintéticas. No menciona aranceles ni normas de seguridad, y las fibras eran sintéticas, no naturales.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o no se dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The Rana Plaza collapse took place in India in 2013.
preguntas.cita: In 2013, the Rana Plaza collapse in Bangladesh, the deadliest garment-related accident in world history
preguntas.explicacion: El año es correcto, pero el derrumbe ocurrió en Bangladés, no en la India.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 11 una palabra que signifique «apodado, bautizado como».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning “given the name of, called”.
preguntas.cita: This phenomenon has been dubbed ultra-fast fashion.
preguntas.explicacion: «To dub» significa poner un apodo o nombre; aquí, el fenómeno se ha bautizado como moda ultrarrápida.

preguntas.pregunta: According to the United Nations Environment Programme, consumers today…
opciones: buy about 60% more clothing and keep it about half as long
buy about 60% more clothing and keep it twice as long
buy about half as much clothing but replace it more often
buy about 36% more clothing and keep it half as long
respuestas: buy about 60% more clothing and keep it about half as long
preguntas.cita: consumers are buying approximately 60% more clothing than in the past while keeping garments for about half as long
preguntas.explicacion: El PNUMA habla de un 60 % más de compras y de la mitad de tiempo de uso. El 36 % es la cuota de mercado de la moda rápida, no el aumento de compras.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o no se dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Natural fibres such as cotton release no microplastics at all.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto solo habla de la liberación de microplásticos por las prendas sintéticas. No dice nada sobre el algodón ni otras fibras naturales.

preguntas.pregunta: Why are fast-fashion garments associated with particularly high releases of microplastics?
respuestas: Because synthetic fabrics shed more fibres in their first washes, and fast-fashion clothes are used for short periods and wear out quickly, so many new garments go through those first washes and are soon discarded.
preguntas.cita: synthetic fabrics tend to shed more fibres during their first washes, while these garments are generally used for shorter periods and often wear out quickly
preguntas.explicacion: Hay que combinar dos causas: las primeras coladas sueltan más fibras y las prendas duran poco, por lo que se renuevan con frecuencia.

preguntas.pregunta: Why was Shein fined in Italy?
opciones: For misleading environmental claims about its products
For copying the designs of major brands
For poor working conditions in its factories
For using PFAS in its clothing
respuestas: For misleading environmental claims about its products
preguntas.cita: Shein was fined €1m in Italy for misleading environmental claims about products.
preguntas.explicacion: La multa italiana fue por afirmaciones ambientales engañosas (greenwashing). Las copias de diseños se tratan en otro párrafo y no se mencionan multas por PFAS ni por condiciones laborales a Shein.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 18 una palabra que signifique «infractor» (de derechos de propiedad intelectual).
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning “someone who violates a right or law”.
preguntas.cita: Shein is considered to be the most frequent infringer
preguntas.explicacion: «Infringer» es quien vulnera un derecho; «infringement» es la infracción, sobre todo de patentes o derechos de autor.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o no se dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The French law banned all advertising of ultra-fast fashion as soon as it took effect in September 2026.
preguntas.cita: Beginning 1 January 2027, the law will also ban all advertising of ultra-fast fashion, including influencer marketing.
preguntas.explicacion: La ley entró en vigor en septiembre de 2026, pero la prohibición de la publicidad empieza el 1 de enero de 2027.

preguntas.pregunta: On what grounds did China and some French lawmakers criticise the French law?
respuestas: China argued that it was a discriminatory trade restriction aimed at Chinese firms and threatened retaliation, whereas some French MPs complained that it had been watered down so as not to target French and European brands.
preguntas.cita: arguing that it was a discriminatory trade restriction
preguntas.explicacion: Las críticas van en sentidos opuestos: China la considera discriminatoria; algunos diputados franceses, demasiado suave con las empresas europeas.

opciones: Advertising for high-carbon products on city-controlled spaces
The sale of ultra-fast fashion in the city
All advertising at bus stops
Influencer marketing of clothing
respuestas: Advertising for high-carbon products on city-controlled spaces
preguntas.cita: passed a bylaw banning advertising for “high-carbon” products on city-controlled advertising spaces
preguntas.explicacion: La norma de Bristol prohíbe anunciar productos de alta huella de carbono en espacios municipales. No prohíbe la venta ni toda la publicidad, y la prohibición de influencers corresponde a la ley francesa.

tribunal.pregunta: How would you define fast fashion, and what distinguishes ultra-fast fashion from it?
tribunal.pista_es: Definir el modelo y explicar el salto de velocidad que traen las redes sociales.
ideas: Rapid copying of trends at low prices
Flexible supply chains and small batches
Ultra-fast fashion: social media, even shorter cycles, lower quality

tribunal.pregunta: What are the main environmental costs of fast fashion mentioned in the text?
tribunal.pista_es: Enumerar residuos, agua, contaminación química, emisiones y microplásticos.

tribunal.pregunta: Why do you think consumers keep buying fast fashion despite its social and environmental impact?
tribunal.pista_es: Dar una opinión razonada sobre precios, marketing y comportamiento del consumidor.
ideas: Externalities are not reflected in prices

tribunal.pregunta: Spanish groups such as Inditex are among the leaders of this industry. What does fast fashion mean for the Spanish economy?
tribunal.pista_es: Relacionar el texto con el peso de Inditex y la cadena de valor textil en España.
ideas: Inditex's global expansion and proximity sourcing

tribunal.pregunta: Is a levy on each garment, as in the French law, an efficient way to correct the externalities of fast fashion?
tribunal.pista_es: Analizar la medida desde la economía pública (impuesto pigouviano) y sus límites.
ideas: A Pigouvian tax internalises environmental costs
Risk of regressive effects on low-income consumers

tribunal.pregunta: China called the French law a discriminatory trade restriction. Do you think it is compatible with WTO rules?
tribunal.pista_es: Valorar la ley a la luz del principio de no discriminación y las excepciones ambientales del GATT.
ideas: The law applies on volume criteria, not origin
Risk of retaliation and trade tensions

tribunal.pregunta: Should this kind of regulation be adopted at EU level rather than by individual member states?
tribunal.pista_es: Relacionar con la estrategia textil de la UE, el mercado único y la competencia en materia comercial.
ideas: Avoiding fragmentation of the single market
EU Strategy for Sustainable and Circular Textiles
Customs treatment of low-value parcels from e-commerce platforms
